more","cards":[],"body":{"text":"My sister's son potty trained in 1 week. My son took almost a year. And it drove me crazy…

But it turns out, she had something up her sleeve the whole time.

A potty training cheat code that could have saved me months of stress… but I was too stubborn to ask.

Because my sister and I have been super competitive our whole lives.

Sports. Grades. Board games. It didn't matter, I always tried to beat her at everything. And I usually did…

But when it came to potty training… she completely outdid me.

Last year, my sister and I started potty training at the same time.

Both of our sons are the same age, so of course it became a competition.

I bought the rewards, the sticker charts, the fancy potty, everything I could to give myself the best chance.

We even started on the exact same day.

Day 2, she texts me: "Theo sat on the potty for the first time today! He's picking it up now!"

My son Blair peed on the floor 5 times and pooped twice that day.

I texted back: "Wow that's so good. Keep it up."

But I'd be lying if I said I was actually thrilled about it.

Day 5, another text: "He's sitting on the potty most of the time now. Only one or two accidents."

Our day 5? Tears. Tantrums. Puddles on the floor.

I didn't even respond to her message.

A few weeks later, we were at a family BBQ.

Theo runs up to my sister and says "Mommy I'm going to potty now."

He takes himself to the potty completely on his own.

Blair? Still in disposables.

My sister had this smug look on her face. I didn't even want to make eye contact. I couldn't bear it.

We left early that night, and on the drive home I didn't say a word. Just stared out the window feeling completely defeated.

They were the same age. They started on the exact same day. So why did her son train in a week and mine is still in diapers?

So I kept at it. Every day for months.

The Oh Crap method. The 3-day method. Encouragement.

Still multiple accidents a day.

He'd say he didn't need to go then I'd turn around to him standing in a puddle of pee.

We were ten and a half months in now and still no progress. I was exhausted.

The daily routines. The methods. The cost of pull-ups adding up every month. And I still had nothing to show for it.

So I did the one thing I'd been avoiding for months… I FaceTimed my sister.

How did you do it? I asked her. How did you potty train so fast?

She laughed. "Honestly, I can't take the credit for it. All I did was change what he was wearing."

She explained how she had spoken to a child development expert before starting, who had told her that diapers can prolong potty training.

They absorb moisture in seconds so kids can't actually feel their accidents. And if they can't feel it, they can't learn. They stay bone dry, so their brain gets no feedback that they've peed.

He said that the solution is to remove the disposables immediately.

But don't just switch to regular underwear. Because while they do help kids feel wet, they just soak through and ruin their clothes or your furniture.

You need a specific type of underwear for potty training.

Ones that help kids feel wet while keeping everything contained.

They're called UpAiry training pants.

They have this special Feel & Learn technology that holds wetness against the skin, sending a signal to the brain and providing sensory feedback.

But the outer layer is leak resistant so they don't soak through.

I just stared at her through the phone.

Ten and a half months. That's how long I'd been avoiding this call.

She wasn't smarter than me. She wasn't a better parent than me. She just knew something I didn't.

That's why Blair would say he didn't need to go then pee on the floor right after. I was asking him to recognize something he couldn't feel.

So I ordered them.

Day 1: Blair was playing with his blocks when he just stopped. He ran to me and said "Mommy, I feel something."

He peed and he could feel it on his skin. For the first time he was starting to recognize it.

Day 4: He sat on the potty and peed. Still a few accidents throughout the day, but now he was starting to realize that using the potty could stop the yucky wet feeling.

Day 9: He was using the potty EVERY TIME.

No accidents. No puddles. Nothing.

I FaceTimed my sister again and thanked her. We just laughed.

It was such a relief.

I didn't even care that my sister had beaten me at something (for the first time btw). I was just so glad to be diaper free.

So if you're potty training right now, and it's taking longer than expected, don't blame yourself, or the methods. Start with what they're wearing.

Diapers and disposables keep kids dry so they can't feel their accidents.

Training pants give their brain the feedback it needs.

That can be the difference between 1 week and 1 year.

Hope this helps another parent out there in the same situation.

details","cards":[],"body":{"text":"Potty training's going about as well as expected.

This is her fourth time on the potty today. 

Fourth time sitting there for fifteen minutes. 

Fourth time getting off and peeing somewhere else within ten minutes.

The carpet. The couch. Inside her rain boot once. I don't even know how that one happened.

She's not upset about it. She's not embarrassed. 

She literally does not know it's happening until she's standing in it.

And I keep thinking okay maybe tomorrow. Maybe next week. Maybe she just needs more time.

But we've been saying that for eight months.

Eight months of her sitting on it, doing nothing, getting off, and going on the floor like the potty doesn't exist.

And now her daycare sent a letter home. 

She needs to be independently toileting by September or she can't move up to the preschool room. 

That gives me nine weeks.

Nine weeks to figure out what eight months couldn't.

So I'm venting to my sister on the phone last night and she goes "have you talked to anyone who actually knows why this happens? 

Not just how to do it but why it's not working?"

And I'm like... no? The pediatrician said she's fine. 

The internet says be consistent. I've been consistent for EIGHT MONTHS.

So she sends me this account — a child development woman who works specifically with kids who've been stuck in potty training for months. 

Not a potty training "coach" selling a course. Someone who actually explains the science of why some kids can't figure it out.

And I watched one of her videos and she said something that made me feel physically sick.

She said "If your child sits on the potty and nothing happens, then pees five minutes later with no warning — they're not being difficult. 

They cannot feel the urge building. Their brain is not receiving the signal."

And I'm like... what?

She said disposables are designed to absorb in under two seconds. 

Skin stays completely dry. So from birth, every single time the child pees, their brain gets zero feedback. 

No wetness. No discomfort. Nothing changes.

And after two, three years of that — the brain stops paying attention to the bladder signal entirely. 

It's like wearing noise-cancelling headphones since birth. The sound is still there. The nerve still fires. 

But the brain has learned to ignore it because it never leads to anything.

That's why she sits on the potty and nothing happens. She can't feel that her bladder is full. The signal isn't reaching her brain.

And that's why she pees five minutes later with no warning — because by the time it finally breaks through, it's already happening.

She's not holding it. She's not refusing. She genuinely cannot feel it coming.

And every method I've tried — the timer, the stickers, Oh Crap, the naked weekend — all of them assume she can already feel the urge and just needs to learn what to do with it.

But she can't feel it. So none of them can work. I've been trying to teach her to respond to a signal her brain isn't receiving.

Eight months. Eight months of getting frustrated with her. 

Eight months of "why won't you just GO?" And she couldn't feel it. She couldn't feel it the whole time.

So this woman said you need to restore the signal. 

You need to put them in something where they actually feel wet against their skin the moment it happens. Not to punish them. 

Just to give the brain the information it's been missing.

She said once the brain starts getting feedback again, most kids figure it out within days. 

Not months. Days. Because the pathway is already there — it's just been muted.

But she said you can't just do naked because most people can't sustain it. Pee everywhere. Carpet. Couch. 

You burn out in two days and put them back in disposables and the signal disappears again.

She said you need training pants that feel wet against the skin but contain it. 

So the brain gets the feedback without you losing your house.

She recommended a brand called UpAiry. 

Said they're the only ones she's found where the cotton actually holds wetness against the skin long enough for the brain to register it. 

Most others either leak through or use polyester that doesn't create the sensation.

So I ordered them because honestly what else am I going to do. We have nine weeks. If this doesn't work I'm pulling her from daycare.

They came on a Wednesday.

Thursday morning I put them on her.

By 10am she'd had an accident. But she STOPPED. Mid-play. Looked down. Pulled at the waistband. 

Walked over to me and said "Mommy. Wet."

She has never said that. Not once in eight months. 

In disposables she'd pee and keep coloring without blinking. Now she's stopping. Feeling it. Telling me.

I almost cried right there in the kitchen.

Day 3. One accident in the morning. Then she stood up from her toys, walked to the bathroom, pulled them down, sat on the potty, and went. 

By herself. No timer. No prompt. No M&M.

She just felt it coming and knew what to do.

THE SAME POTTY. The one she's been sitting on for eight months doing nothing. 

She just needed to feel WHY it was there.

Day 5. She started telling me before. "Mommy I need to go." Running to the bathroom. Making it every time.

Week 2. Going on her own. Dry all day.

Week 3. Regular underwear. She picked the ones with strawberries. No accidents in five days.

We're going to make September. 

After eight months of nothing, it took two weeks.

And I'm still not over the fact that nobody — not the pediatrician, not the daycare, not a single one of the fifteen articles I read — ever told me that the thing she was wearing was the thing preventing her from learning.

—

Also my neighbor's son is the same age and stuck in the same place. 

I sent her the link last week. She texted me three days later and said "he stopped playing and looked down and said 'wet.' He's NEVER done that."

Same thing. All he needed was to feel it.

—

If your kid is doing what mine was doing — sitting on the potty, nothing happens, then peeing somewhere else five minutes later like the potty doesn't exist — it's probably not stubbornness. They probably just can't feel it.

I'm talking the kind of laugh where she had to put down her tea.

Not mean.

More like… "Oh, honey, bless your heart."

She pointed at the $40 box in my cart.

"You teach him to pee in his pants for two years… then wonder why he won't use the potty?"

I didn't know what to say. Because she was right. That's literally what I'd been doing.

She invited me over the next day. Sat me down. And explained something I'd never heard from any pediatrician or parenting book.

In traditional Chinese culture, babies are potty-trained before they can walk.

Not at 2 years old.

Not at 3.

Before their first birthday.

She showed me old photos of her own kids wearing these little pants with no crotch.

They're called kai dang ku.

Split pants.

When a baby needs to pee, they squat.

Right there.

Wherever they are.

And they FEEL it.

The wetness. The sensation. The connection between "I need to go" and "this is what happens."

Their bodies learn the pattern immediately.

No diapers blocking the feedback.

No waiting for some magical "readiness" age.

Just biology doing what it's always done.

She said in China, a 3-year-old still in diapers would be shocking.

Not because the parents are better. Because the METHOD is different. And suddenly, everything made sense.

Western parents spend years teaching their kids that it's OKAY to pee in their pants.

We put them in diapers that wick away moisture so fast they don't feel a thing.

No feedback.

No consequence.

No reason for their brain to connect the dots.

Then one day we decide they're "ready"...

And we expect them to UNLEARN two or three years of conditioning.

Of course, it's a battle.

Of course, they resist.

We're asking them to reverse something we spent their whole life teaching them.

The problem isn't the kid.

It's the method.

I thought about all the times I'd tried to potty train my son.

The sticker charts. The timers. The M&Ms.

The 45-minute sits where he'd do nothing, then pee on the floor five minutes later.

The guilt every time another mom casually mentioned her kid was trained at 18 months.

The growing fear that something was wrong with him. Or worse… with ME.

But according to my mother-in-law, nothing was wrong. I'd just been set up to fail by a system designed to sell diapers.

Not to work with how kids actually learn.

Now here's the problem.

I wasn't about to do full elimination communication.

I'm not following my toddler around the grocery store with a little potty.

I'm not putting him in crotchless pants at the playground.

That's not realistic for American life.

But the IDEA? That part made total sense.

Kids need to FEEL what happens when they pee. That's how their body learns.

Western diapers block that feedback. So the learning never happens.

My mother-in-law shrugged when I explained I couldn't go full traditional.

"You don't need to," she said.

"You just need to give him the feeling back."

So I started looking for something that would.

Disposables didn't work. They're just diapers with better marketing.

Going commando seemed like a nightmare for my couch.

Then I found UpAiry.

It's training underwear that works on the same principle as those split pants.

When your kid pees, they feel it immediately. The wetness doesn't get wicked away. It sits there long enough for their brain to register: "This doesn't feel right."

But it's contained enough that you don't have to clean pee off your furniture three times a day.

It's the ancient method made practical for modern parents.

The bridge between 2,000-year-old wisdom and a Target-shopping lifestyle.

We tried it.

The first few days were rough.

My son had accidents. But he NOTICED them. He'd stop playing, look down, tug at his pants.

That had never happened in disposables.

By day three, he was coming to me when he felt wet.

By day five, he was asking to sit on the potty.

By day eight, he was pulling down his UpAirys and going on his own.

No bribes. No battles. No sticker charts or timers or desperate negotiations.

Just his body finally getting the information it needed to make the connection.

The power struggle disappeared. Because I wasn't fighting biology anymore. I was working with it.

Here's what nobody tells you.

The "wait until they're ready" timeline? That's a Western invention.

It's not a biological law.

Billions of people across thousands of years have potty-trained their kids way earlier using this exact principle.

The only reason we think 3 years old is normal…

Is because the diaper industry made a lot of money convincing us to wait.

You don't have to keep waiting.

You don't have to keep fighting with a method that was designed to fail.

You can restore the feedback loop that's been working since before diapers even existed.

UpAiry gives you 75 days to try it risk-free.

If the ancient principle doesn't work for your kid, you're covered.

But if it does… You'll finally understand why my mother-in-law was laughing.

Because the solution was always simpler than the modern parenting industry wanted us to believe.

You weren't behind. You weren't failing. You were just using a broken method that fights against how humans actually learn.

And now you know there's a better way.

One that's been proven for 2,000 years.

You just needed someone to tell you it existed.

If you're in the thick of this right now, I can't recommend UpAiry enough.

It gave me my life back.

Not in some vague "self-care" way.

In a real, tangible, I-can-think-clearly-again way.

details","cards":[],"body":{"text":"Potty training's going about as well as expected.

This is her fourth time on the potty today. 

Fourth time sitting there for fifteen minutes. 

Fourth time getting off and peeing somewhere else within ten minutes.

The carpet. The couch. Inside her rain boot once. I don't even know how that one happened.

She's not upset about it. She's not embarrassed. 

She literally does not know it's happening until she's standing in it.

And I keep thinking okay maybe tomorrow. Maybe next week. Maybe she just needs more time.

But we've been saying that for eight months.

Eight months of her sitting on it, doing nothing, getting off, and going on the floor like the potty doesn't exist.

And now her daycare sent a letter home. 

She needs to be independently toileting by September or she can't move up to the preschool room. 

That gives me nine weeks.

Nine weeks to figure out what eight months couldn't.

So I'm venting to my sister on the phone last night and she goes "have you talked to anyone who actually knows why this happens? 

Not just how to do it but why it's not working?"

And I'm like... no? The pediatrician said she's fine. 

The internet says be consistent. I've been consistent for EIGHT MONTHS.

So she sends me this account — a child development woman who works specifically with kids who've been stuck in potty training for months. 

Not a potty training "coach" selling a course. Someone who actually explains the science of why some kids can't figure it out.

And I watched one of her videos and she said something that made me feel physically sick.

She said "If your child sits on the potty and nothing happens, then pees five minutes later with no warning — they're not being difficult. 

They cannot feel the urge building. Their brain is not receiving the signal."

And I'm like... what?

She said disposables are designed to absorb in under two seconds. 

Skin stays completely dry. So from birth, every single time the child pees, their brain gets zero feedback. 

No wetness. No discomfort. Nothing changes.

And after two, three years of that — the brain stops paying attention to the bladder signal entirely. 

It's like wearing noise-cancelling headphones since birth. The sound is still there. The nerve still fires. 

But the brain has learned to ignore it because it never leads to anything.

That's why she sits on the potty and nothing happens. She can't feel that her bladder is full. The signal isn't reaching her brain.

And that's why she pees five minutes later with no warning — because by the time it finally breaks through, it's already happening.

She's not holding it. She's not refusing. She genuinely cannot feel it coming.

And every method I've tried — the timer, the stickers, Oh Crap, the naked weekend — all of them assume she can already feel the urge and just needs to learn what to do with it.

But she can't feel it. So none of them can work. I've been trying to teach her to respond to a signal her brain isn't receiving.

Eight months. Eight months of getting frustrated with her. 

Eight months of "why won't you just GO?" And she couldn't feel it. She couldn't feel it the whole time.

So this woman said you need to restore the signal. 

You need to put them in something where they actually feel wet against their skin the moment it happens. Not to punish them. 

Just to give the brain the information it's been missing.

She said once the brain starts getting feedback again, most kids figure it out within days. 

Not months. Days. Because the pathway is already there — it's just been muted.

But she said you can't just do naked because most people can't sustain it. Pee everywhere. Carpet. Couch. 

You burn out in two days and put them back in disposables and the signal disappears again.

She said you need training pants that feel wet against the skin but contain it. 

So the brain gets the feedback without you losing your house.

She recommended a brand called UpAiry. 

Said they're the only ones she's found where the cotton actually holds wetness against the skin long enough for the brain to register it. 

Most others either leak through or use polyester that doesn't create the sensation.

So I ordered them because honestly what else am I going to do. We have nine weeks. If this doesn't work I'm pulling her from daycare.

They came on a Wednesday.

Thursday morning I put them on her.

By 10am she'd had an accident. But she STOPPED. Mid-play. Looked down. Pulled at the waistband. 

Walked over to me and said "Mommy. Wet."

She has never said that. Not once in eight months. 

In disposables she'd pee and keep coloring without blinking. Now she's stopping. Feeling it. Telling me.

I almost cried right there in the kitchen.

Day 3. One accident in the morning. Then she stood up from her toys, walked to the bathroom, pulled them down, sat on the potty, and went. 

By herself. No timer. No prompt. No M&M.

She just felt it coming and knew what to do.

THE SAME POTTY. The one she's been sitting on for eight months doing nothing. 

She just needed to feel WHY it was there.

Day 5. She started telling me before. "Mommy I need to go." Running to the bathroom. Making it every time.

Week 2. Going on her own. Dry all day.

Week 3. Regular underwear. She picked the ones with strawberries. No accidents in five days.

We're going to make September. 

After eight months of nothing, it took two weeks.

And I'm still not over the fact that nobody — not the pediatrician, not the daycare, not a single one of the fifteen articles I read — ever told me that the thing she was wearing was the thing preventing her from learning.

—

Also my neighbor's son is the same age and stuck in the same place. 

I sent her the link last week. She texted me three days later and said "he stopped playing and looked down and said 'wet.' He's NEVER done that."

Same thing. All he needed was to feel it.

—

My name is Bec. I'm 31 years old. I work full-time in marketing.

For the past 2 years, everyone kept telling me 

"you need to take time off work to potty train."

"You need 3-5 days straight at home with no interruptions."

"Working moms can't do this the same way stay-at-home moms can."

So I kept waiting for the "right time."

Waiting for a week off. Waiting for her to get older so it would be faster. Waiting for it to somehow get easier.

Meanwhile she turned 3. Then 3 and a half. Then 4.

And I kept thinking "when I have time off work, we'll do it then."

But I never had that time.

And last month, my mother-in-law came over for dinner.

She watched me change my daughter's diaper after bath time.

"You know, in my day, mothers stayed home. My kids were all trained by 18 months."

She didn't say it mean. Just... matter-of-fact.

Like of course I'm struggling. I work. Husband doesn't really help. What did I expect?

Because she's right, isn't she?

If I'd stayed home like my mom did. Like her mom did. Like 84% of moms did in the 1950s.

Maybe this wouldn't be so hard.

—

Two weeks ago I was up late googling "how to potty train while working full-time."

Desperate for some method that worked with my schedule.

And I found a study from the UK that made me stop scrolling.

62% of working parents in the UK delayed starting potty training because they couldn't commit to a structured schedule.

I sat there staring at that number.

62%.

I'm not alone. Most working parents are doing exactly what I did.

Delaying. Waiting. Hoping it gets easier later.

But then I kept reading.

The study said delaying made it harder, not easier.

Kids who started training after age 3 took significantly longer than kids who started at 18-24 months.

Wait, what?

I delayed specifically so it would be faster when I finally had time.

But delaying made it slower?

And then I found another stat that actually pissed me off.

"In the 1940s and 50s, 92% of children were potty trained by 18 months. Today, the average is 35-39 months."

So kids used to train at 18 months when 84% of moms stayed home.

Now kids train at 35+ months when 70% of moms work.

Everyone says it's because we don't have time.

And I believed that.

That's why I delayed.

But then I found this comment thread that made me question everything.

Someone wrote: "My friend is a stay-at-home mom. She's been trying to train her 3.5-year-old for over a year. Still stuck. If it was just about having time, she'd be done by now."

Another person: "I work full-time. Trained my kid in 2 weeks. My sister stays home. Took her 18 months. Time isn't the only factor."

Wait.

If stay-at-home moms with unlimited time are struggling for years...

And some working moms with no time are succeeding in weeks...

What's the actual difference?

—

So I went down a complete rabbit hole that night.

And I found a thread where a child psychologist was explaining delayed potty training.

She said yes, working parents often delay starting because they don't have time for traditional methods.

But delaying isn't the main problem.

The main problem is what kids are wearing during all those extra months and years.

She explained something called operant conditioning.

It's how all learning works.

You do something, you feel a result, your brain connects the two.

Touch hot stove → feel pain → learn don't touch again.

Pee in pants → feel wetness → learn use potty instead.

But disposable diapers break that learning loop completely.

When toddlers pee in a disposable, it absorbs in 2-3 seconds.

They never feel wet. Never uncomfortable. Never feel anything.

So their brain never connects "I peed" with "something happened."

She called this sensory erasure.

The learning signal gets erased before the brain can process it.

Like trying to teach a kid not to touch a hot stove that never gets hot.

They'd keep touching it forever because there's no consequence to learn from.

And here's what hit me hard.

She said: "There's a critical window between 18-30 months when the brain is naturally wired to learn this connection. By keeping kids in disposables past age 3, you're not just delaying—you're working against their brain's natural development window."

My daughter is 4.

I kept her in disposables for 2 extra years thinking I was waiting for the right time.

But I wasn't just delaying the skill.

I was letting the learning window close while she spent years learning to ignore the signal.

—

Then she said:

"Yes, more moms stayed home in the 1950s. But those moms also used cloth diapers that stayed wet for hours."

"Kids felt it immediately. Their brain made the connection fast."

"Today's working parents don't have time. And today's stay-at-home parents are using disposables that erase feedback."

"Neither group has the full advantage 1950s moms had: time plus sensory feedback."

"But here's what most people miss: sensory feedback matters more than time."

"A working parent with 2 hours a day and the right materials will succeed faster than a stay-at-home parent with unlimited time and wrong materials."

And I just sat there.

I blamed myself for working.

Blamed myself for not having time.

Delayed for 2 years because I thought I needed weeks off work.

But stay-at-home moms with all the time in the world were stuck too.

Because we're ALL using materials that block learning.

Time doesn't matter if the signal is erased.

The psychologist said the solution isn't quitting your job or taking weeks off.

It's using training pants that restore sensory feedback.

When kids pee in them, they feel it immediately.

But the outer layer contains it so you're not cleaning puddles.

That immediate feedback is what creates learning—even with limited time.

She specifically mentioned UpAiry training pants.

Said they're designed to create strong sensory feedback that disposables erase.

And that working parents often see fast results because the feedback is so clear during their limited time together.

I looked them up at 1am.

Reviews from working moms:

"I only have 2 hours a day with my daughter. These worked in 10 days."

"Trained in 2 weeks working full-time. My SAHM friend took 6 months."

I ordered them that night.

—

When they arrived, I put them on my daughter after I picked her up from daycare.

That evening, she had 2 accidents in our 3 hours together.

But both times, she stopped immediately.

"Mommy, I'm wet."

In 4 years—four years—she'd never said that.

She'd just keep playing in disposables. Zero awareness.

But these? She felt it the second it happened.

Day 2, one accident during our evening time. Told me right away.

Day 3, she was playing with blocks. Suddenly stopped.

"Mommy, I feel something weird."

We ran to the bathroom. She went.

Her eyes went huge. "That's what it feels like before?"

Four years old. First time she'd ever felt the urge before it happened.

Week one, she started telling me before most accidents during our evening time.

Daycare said she was doing the same there during the day.

Her brain was finally connecting sensation to action.

Week two, making it to the potty almost every time.

Week three, fully dry for 5 days straight. At daycare and at home.

My husband said "Wait, she's actually trained? Already?"

I said "Yeah. Because she could finally feel what was happening."

—

I texted my mother-in-law: "Emma's fully trained."

She called me: "Oh wonderful! Did you take time off work?"

I said "No. I work the same hours. Just changed what she was wearing."

Silence.

Then: "Well... that's wonderful, honey."

—

Also!! I posted about this in a moms group.

Four other moms messaged me saying the exact same thing.

"I delayed starting because I don't have time off work."

"Everyone told me I needed to stay home for days straight."

"My kid is 4+ and I keep waiting for a better time."

I sent them the link.

Two weeks later, all four said something like: "It worked. Even with my work schedule."

—

Look, the stat is true: 70% of moms work today versus 16% in the 1950s.

We absolutely have less time than our mothers and grandmothers did.

And that makes traditional potty training methods nearly impossible.

But here's what everyone misses:

1950s moms had time plus cloth diapers.

We lost the time advantage.

But we also lost the sensory feedback advantage.

And sensory feedback matters more than time.

I delayed for 2 years thinking I needed weeks off work.

But I didn't need more time.

I needed materials that created feedback during the limited time I had.

These training pants worked because my daughter could finally feel what was happening.

Even in just 2-3 hours a day.

Even with me working 45 hours a week.

Even without taking any time off.

The learning loop finally completed: Pee → Feel wet → Learn to use potty.

And once that signal reached her brain?

Three weeks.

After 2 years of delaying because I thought I didn't have time.

Turns out I didn't need more time.

I just needed the right materials during the time I had.

And everyone's right—we don't have time to potty train the way they did back then.

I work 45 hours a week. I have maybe 3 hours with my daughter on weeknights after pickup.

So I kept delaying. 

"I'll start when I have more time." 
"I'll wait until she's older." 
"I need days off work to do this right."

And now she's 4 years old. Still in diapers. And I'm sitting here absolutely furious.

My name is Bec. I'm 31 years old. I work full-time in marketing.

For the past 2 years, everyone kept telling me 

"you need to take time off work to potty train."

"You need 3-5 days straight at home with no interruptions."

"Working moms can't do this the same way stay-at-home moms can."

So I kept waiting for the "right time."

Waiting for a week off. Waiting for her to get older so it would be faster. Waiting for it to somehow get easier.

Meanwhile she turned 3. Then 3 and a half. Then 4.

And I kept thinking "when I have time off work, we'll do it then."

But I never had that time.

And last month, my mother-in-law came over for dinner.

She watched me change my daughter's diaper after bath time.

"You know, in my day, mothers stayed home. My kids were all trained by 18 months."

She didn't say it mean. Just... matter-of-fact.

Like of course I'm struggling. I work. Husband doesn't really help. What did I expect?

Because she's right, isn't she?

If I'd stayed home like my mom did. Like her mom did. Like 84% of moms did in the 1950s.

Maybe this wouldn't be so hard.

—

Two weeks ago I was up late googling "how to potty train while working full-time."

Desperate for some method that worked with my schedule.

And I found a study from the UK that made me stop scrolling.

62% of working parents in the UK delayed starting potty training because they couldn't commit to a structured schedule.

I sat there staring at that number.

62%.

I'm not alone. Most working parents are doing exactly what I did.

Delaying. Waiting. Hoping it gets easier later.

But then I kept reading.

The study said delaying made it harder, not easier.

Kids who started training after age 3 took significantly longer than kids who started at 18-24 months.

Wait, what?

I delayed specifically so it would be faster when I finally had time.

But delaying made it slower?

And then I found another stat that actually pissed me off.

"In the 1940s and 50s, 92% of children were potty trained by 18 months. Today, the average is 35-39 months."

So kids used to train at 18 months when 84% of moms stayed home.

Now kids train at 35+ months when 70% of moms work.

Everyone says it's because we don't have time.

And I believed that.

That's why I delayed.

But then I found this comment thread that made me question everything.

Someone wrote: "My friend is a stay-at-home mom. She's been trying to train her 3.5-year-old for over a year. Still stuck. If it was just about having time, she'd be done by now."

Another person: "I work full-time. Trained my kid in 2 weeks. My sister stays home. Took her 18 months. Time isn't the only factor."

Wait.

If stay-at-home moms with unlimited time are struggling for years...

And some working moms with no time are succeeding in weeks...

What's the actual difference?

—

So I went down a complete rabbit hole that night.

And I found a thread where a child psychologist was explaining delayed potty training.

She said yes, working parents often delay starting because they don't have time for traditional methods.

But delaying isn't the main problem.

The main problem is what kids are wearing during all those extra months and years.

She explained something called operant conditioning.

It's how all learning works.

You do something, you feel a result, your brain connects the two.

Touch hot stove → feel pain → learn don't touch again.

Pee in pants → feel wetness → learn use potty instead.

But disposable diapers break that learning loop completely.

When toddlers pee in a disposable, it absorbs in 2-3 seconds.

They never feel wet. Never uncomfortable. Never feel anything.

So their brain never connects "I peed" with "something happened."

She called this sensory erasure.

The learning signal gets erased before the brain can process it.

Like trying to teach a kid not to touch a hot stove that never gets hot.

They'd keep touching it forever because there's no consequence to learn from.

And here's what hit me hard.

She said: "There's a critical window between 18-30 months when the brain is naturally wired to learn this connection. By keeping kids in disposables past age 3, you're not just delaying—you're working against their brain's natural development window."

My daughter is 4.

I kept her in disposables for 2 extra years thinking I was waiting for the right time.

But I wasn't just delaying the skill.

I was letting the learning window close while she spent years learning to ignore the signal.

—

Then she said:

"Yes, more moms stayed home in the 1950s. But those moms also used cloth diapers that stayed wet for hours."

"Kids felt it immediately. Their brain made the connection fast."

"Today's working parents don't have time. And today's stay-at-home parents are using disposables that erase feedback."

"Neither group has the full advantage 1950s moms had: time plus sensory feedback."

"But here's what most people miss: sensory feedback matters more than time."

"A working parent with 2 hours a day and the right materials will succeed faster than a stay-at-home parent with unlimited time and wrong materials."

And I just sat there.

I blamed myself for working.

Blamed myself for not having time.

Delayed for 2 years because I thought I needed weeks off work.

But stay-at-home moms with all the time in the world were stuck too.

Because we're ALL using materials that block learning.

Time doesn't matter if the signal is erased.

The psychologist said the solution isn't quitting your job or taking weeks off.

It's using training pants that restore sensory feedback.

When kids pee in them, they feel it immediately.

But the outer layer contains it so you're not cleaning puddles.

That immediate feedback is what creates learning—even with limited time.

She specifically mentioned UpAiry training pants.

Said they're designed to create strong sensory feedback that disposables erase.

And that working parents often see fast results because the feedback is so clear during their limited time together.

I looked them up at 1am.

Reviews from working moms:

"I only have 2 hours a day with my daughter. These worked in 10 days."

"Trained in 2 weeks working full-time. My SAHM friend took 6 months."

I ordered them that night.

—

When they arrived, I put them on my daughter after I picked her up from daycare.

That evening, she had 2 accidents in our 3 hours together.

But both times, she stopped immediately.

"Mommy, I'm wet."

In 4 years—four years—she'd never said that.

She'd just keep playing in disposables. Zero awareness.

But these? She felt it the second it happened.

Day 2, one accident during our evening time. Told me right away.

Day 3, she was playing with blocks. Suddenly stopped.

"Mommy, I feel something weird."

We ran to the bathroom. She went.

Her eyes went huge. "That's what it feels like before?"

Four years old. First time she'd ever felt the urge before it happened.

Week one, she started telling me before most accidents during our evening time.

Daycare said she was doing the same there during the day.

Her brain was finally connecting sensation to action.

Week two, making it to the potty almost every time.

Week three, fully dry for 5 days straight. At daycare and at home.

My husband said "Wait, she's actually trained? Already?"

I said "Yeah. Because she could finally feel what was happening."

—

I texted my mother-in-law: "Emma's fully trained."

She called me: "Oh wonderful! Did you take time off work?"

I said "No. I work the same hours. Just changed what she was wearing."

Silence.

Then: "Well... that's wonderful, honey."

—

Also!! I posted about this in a moms group.

Four other moms messaged me saying the exact same thing.

"I delayed starting because I don't have time off work."

"Everyone told me I needed to stay home for days straight."

"My kid is 4+ and I keep waiting for a better time."

I sent them the link.

Two weeks later, all four said something like: "It worked. Even with my work schedule."

—

Look, the stat is true: 70% of moms work today versus 16% in the 1950s.

We absolutely have less time than our mothers and grandmothers did.

And that makes traditional potty training methods nearly impossible.

But here's what everyone misses:

1950s moms had time plus cloth diapers.

We lost the time advantage.

But we also lost the sensory feedback advantage.

And sensory feedback matters more than time.

I delayed for 2 years thinking I needed weeks off work.

But I didn't need more time.

I needed materials that created feedback during the limited time I had.

These training pants worked because my daughter could finally feel what was happening.

Even in just 2-3 hours a day.

Even with me working 45 hours a week.

Even without taking any time off.

The learning loop finally completed: Pee → Feel wet → Learn to use potty.

And once that signal reached her brain?

Three weeks.

After 2 years of delaying because I thought I didn't have time.

Turns out I didn't need more time.

I just needed the right materials during the time I had.
